summary: Pan Am is a worker-placement/bidding game where players bid on airport and destination cards to build air routes, buy planes, sell routes to Pan Am for cash, and funnel that money into buying Pan Am stock, with the retro aviation theme woven tightly into the mechanics. Most of the tension comes from an open-bidding worker placement track rather than direct route conflict, and reviewers consistently call it a tight, well-paced design that punches above its "mass market" origins, though the payoff is narrower than the theme suggests since it all reduces to who holds the most stock at the end.
praised: The open-bidding/auction take on worker placement, widely called the standout mechanic and more interactive than typical worker placement
Strong theme integration - route building, plane upgrades, and Pan Am's expansion feel thematically coherent (some reviewers read it as a comment on startups being absorbed by a giant corporation)
Attractive retro aesthetic, accessible iconography (colorblind-friendly icons, textured plane pieces for visually impaired players)
Approachable for newer players while still offering enough depth/multiple viable strategies to reward veterans and repeat plays
criticised: Stock price randomness/Event card swings can unfairly punish players who invest heavily in shares early if the price stays low
Directive/Event card draws add randomness some reviewers felt was unnecessary, with house-rule suggestions to draft instead of draw
Feels flat or lackluster at 2 players since bidding tension depends on more competitors
Component quality criticized by some as cheap for the price - small hard-to-read destination cards, similar card colors for different regions, lightweight plastic pieces
Ultimately most decisions funnel into a single money/stock-accumulation race, so despite thematic variety the actual win condition is narrow

interaction.kind: bidding against each other for routes and landing rights
interaction.detail: Core turns are auctions where players directly bid against one another for exclusive routes, planes, and stock, so winning something is defined by denying it to opponents. Stock holding and investing in the shared Pan Am company add further zero-sum competition over the same limited pool of value.
interaction.said: Marketed and reviewed around 'outbid rivals for lucrative landing rights' — auction-driven economic games in this vein are typically called cutthroat, since every route you win is a route someone else didn't get.

sources: cash from selling routes to Pan Am
dividends from Pan Am stock holdings
scoring.how_you_win: Bid for landing rights, fly routes for income, and sell routes or buy Pan Am stock for payouts; the player with the most money after the four eras wins.
